## 8.3.5.2 NVMe In-band Authentication The **AUTHREQ** field in the Connect response capsule (Figure 581) determines if in-band authentication is required: - If any bit in AUTHREQ is set to '1', the host **must authenticate** on that queue to proceed with Fabrics, Admin, and I/O commands. - Authentication success is defined by the specific security protocol used. - Commands other than Connect, Authentication Send, or Authentication Receive received before authentication success result in an **Authentication Required** status and command abortion. - If all bits in AUTHREQ are '0', authentication is not required, and the controller **shall not abort** commands with Authentication Required status. ### Reauthentication - Hosts may initiate reauthentication at any time; prior authentication remains valid. - If reauthentication results in **AUTH_Failure1** (controller), the controller terminates all commands with **Operation Denied** and disconnects the connection. - If **AUTH_Failure2** is sent by the host, the host disconnects the connection. ### Authentication Transaction Timeout - State is **soft-state**. - Timeout occurs if the next command is not received within: - **Keep Alive Timeout** (if Keep Alive Timer is enabled). - **Two minutes** (default timeout, if Keep Alive Timer is disabled). - Timeout results in the **controller discarding** the authentication transaction state (including T ID). - **Initial authentication timeout** → treated as **authentication failure**, resulting in transport connection termination. - **Reauthentication timeout** → commands after timeout are **aborted with Command Sequence Error**. Figure 784 illustrates an example of an authentication transaction for NVMe/TCP. --- ## 8.3.5.2.1 Special Considerations for In-band Authentication of Discovery Subsystems Hosts using security protocols supporting **unidirectional** or **bidirectional authentication** (e.g., DH-HMAC-CHAP) must follow: 1. **Connecting via well-known Discovery Service NQN (`nqn.2014-08.org.nvmexpress.discovery`)**: - If Discovery subsystem **did not request authentication** → **no authentication transaction**. - If Discovery subsystem **requested authentication** → perform **only unidirectional authentication** (Discovery subsystem authenticates the host; host does not authenticate the well-known NQN). 2. **Connecting via unique Discovery Service NQN** (per section 3.1.3.3): - Regardless of authentication request, host may perform **unidirectional or bidirectional authentication** (i.e., host may authenticate the unique Discovery Service NQN). ### Process for Bidirectional Authentication (Figure 785) 1. Connect using well-known Discovery Service NQN. 2. Perform unidirectional authentication. 3. Perform controller initialization (section 3.5). 4. Retrieve unique Discovery Service NQN (section 3.1.3.3). 5. Perform controller shutdown (section 3.6). 6. Reconnect using the unique Discovery Service NQN. 7. Perform bidirectional authentication with the unique NQN. --- ## 8.3.5.2.2 NVMe In-band Authentication Protocol-Specific Requirements Authentication requirements depend on the **SECP field** in the command. - Authentication protocols use **security protocol identifier E9h** (assigned by SPC-5). - Authentication messages are **self-identifying**. - **SPSP0** and **SPSP1** fields in Authentication Send and Receive commands must be set to **01h**. - Authentication messages map to NVMe over Fabrics command/response pairs: - Mapping to **Authentication Send** is shown in Figure 786. - Mapping to **Authentication Receive** is shown in Figure 787. - Security processing (e.g., third-party authentication verification) may delay completion of **Authentication Receive** commands → host should anticipate delays. ### Table 8.3.5.2.2.1: NVMe In-band Authentication Protocol-Specific Requirements (Send) | Field¹ | Value | | :--- | :--- | | SPSPO | 01h | | SPSPI | 01h | | SECP | E9h | | TL | Specifies the amount of data to transfer in bytes | | Notes: | 1. Refer to section 6.2. | ### Table 8.3.5.2.2.2: NVMe In-band Authentication Protocol-Specific Requirements (Receive) | Field¹ | Value | | :--- | :--- | | SPSPO | 01h | | SPSPI | 01h | | SECP | E9h | | AL | Specifies the amount of data to transfer in bytes² | | Notes: | 1. Refer to section 6.1.
2. Size of the largest authentication message that could be received. |

sections.title: Secure_Channel_Concatenation
sections.summary:
# 8.3.5.3 Secure Channel Concatenation

**Purpose**: Secure channel concatenation enables the use of shared key material derived from an authentication transaction on an unsecured Admin Queue to establish a secure channel (e.g., IPsec or TLS) for subsequent Admin and I/O Queues.

**Process**:
- An authentication transaction occurs over an unsecured Admin Queue.
- Shared key material (pre-shared key, PSK) is generated during this transaction.
- The unsecured Admin Queue transport connection is disconnected by the host after the transaction completes.
- The generated PSK is used to establish a secure channel for subsequent Admin Queue(s) and I/O Queues.

**Definition**: The process of generating a PSK over an insecure channel, disconnecting the unsecured connection, and setting up a secure channel using the PSK is called **secure channel concatenation**.

**Example**: Figure 788 illustrates TLS secure channel concatenation for NVMe/TCP:
- Steps 1–7: TLS secure channel concatenation for the Admin Queue.
- Steps 8–13: Setup of TLS secure channels for I/O Queues.

**Prohibition**: Secure channel concatenation is **prohibited** over any secure channel already established in compliance with an NVM Express Transport specification (e.g., NVMe over TCP). If a host requests secure channel concatenation in this scenario, the controller responds as specified in **Section 8.3.5.4.1**.

**Note**: Replacing a PSK for an existing secure channel is **permitted** (refer to Section 8.3.5.4.1).

**Figure**: Figure 788 shows an example of TLS secure channel concatenation with NVMe/TCP.

sections.title: Common_Authentication_Messages
sections.summary:
### 8.3.5.4 Common Authentication Messages

#### 8.3.5.4.1 AUTH_Negotiate Message  
- Sent by host to controller to indicate supported authentication protocols and optional secure channel concatenation.
- **Message format** (Figure 789):  
  - **Bytes 0–7**: Header fields  
    - **Byte 0**: `AUTH_TYPE = 00h` (common messages)  
    - **Byte 1**: `AUTH_ID = 00h` (AUTH Negotiate)  
    - **Bytes 2–3**: Reserved  
    - **Bytes 4–5**: `T_ID` (16-bit transaction identifier)  
    - **Byte 6**: `SC_C` (Secure Channel Concatenation field)  
    - **Byte 7**: `NAPD` (Number of Authentication Protocol Descriptors)  
  - **Bytes 8–71+64×(NAPD−1)**: Authentication Protocol Descriptor List (64 bytes each)  
- **Authentication Protocol Descriptor** (first byte identifies protocol):  
  - `01h`: DH-HMAC-CHAP (only defined currently)  
  - All other values: Reserved  
- **SC_C Values and Rules** (Table 2):  
  - `00h` (NOSC): No secure channel concatenation; allowed on Admin/I/O Queues; does not generate PSK.  
  - `02h` (NEWTLSPSK):  
    - Allowed on Admin Queue over TCP without TLS; generates new PSK.  
    - Prohibited on I/O Queue over TCP without TLS.  
    - Prohibited on Admin/I/O Queue over TLS.  
  - `03h` (REPLACETLSPSK):  
    - Allowed on Admin Queue over TLS; replaces existing PSK.  
    - Prohibited on Admin/I/O Queue over TCP without TLS.  
    - Prohibited on I/O Queue over TLS.  
  - All other values: Reserved  
- **Controller Response** to AUTH_Negotiate:  
  - If `SC_C` does not satisfy controller security requirements or is prohibited for the queue, send `AUTH_Failure1` with reason code `03h` ("Secure channel concatenation mismatch") and disconnect.  
  - If protocol descriptors do not meet security requirements, send `AUTH_Failure1` with reason code `02h` ("Authentication protocol not usable") and disconnect.

#### 8.3.5.4.2 AUTH_Failure Messages  
- **AUTH_Failure1**: Controller → Host (Figure 792)  
- **AUTH_Failure2**: Host → Controller  
- **Message Format** (Table 1):  
  - **Bytes 0–7**:  
    - **Byte 0**: `AUTH_TYPE = 00h`  
    - **Byte 1**: `AUTH_ID = F0h` (AUTH_Failure2), `F1h` (AUTH_Failure1)  
    - **Bytes 2–3**: Reserved  
    - **Bytes 4–5**: `T_ID`  
    - **Byte 6**: `RCODE` (Reason Code)  
    - **Byte 7**: `RCODEEX` (Reason Code Explanation)  
- **Reason Codes** (Table 2):  
  - `01h`: Authentication failure  
  - All other values: Reserved  
- **Reason Code Explanations** (Table 3):  
  - `01h`: Authentication failed  
  - `02h`: Authentication protocol not usable  
  - `03h`: Secure channel concatenation mismatch  
  - `04h`: Hash function not usable  
  - `05h`: DH group not usable  
  - `06h`: Incorrect payload  
  - `07h`: Incorrect protocol message  
  - All other values: Reserved  

#### 8.3.5.4.3 Mapping of Common Authentication Messages to Authentication Commands  
- **AUTH_Negotiate** and **AUTH_Failure2**: Host → Controller → Mapped to **Authentication Send** command.  
- **AUTH_Failure1**: Controller → Host → Mapped to **Authentication Receive** command.

sections.title: DH-HMAC-CHAP_Protocol
sections.summary:
# 8.3.5.5 DH-HMAC-CHAP Protocol

## 8.3.5.5.1 Protocol Operations

DH-HMAC-CHAP is a key-based authentication and key management protocol based on CHAP (RFC 1994), enhanced with HMAC (RFC 2104) using strong hash functions and optional Diffie-Hellman (DH) exchange (RFC 2631, clause 2.2.1). It supports bidirectional or unidirectional authentication between a host and controller. The DH exchange is optional; without it, the protocol reduces to HMAC-CHAP, which is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks if keys are not sufficiently random. All implementations must support DH-HMAC-CHAP with a NULL DH exchange and be configurable to require DH exchange (i.e., prohibit HMAC-CHAP).

Each host and NVM subsystem must have a DH-HMAC-CHAP key associated with its NQN. Impersonation is possible if keys are shared. Authentication requires either:
- Knowing the peer's key, or
- Relying on a third party that knows the key.

Authentication proceeds as:
1. **AUTH_Negotiate**: Host sends transaction identifier (T_ID) and supported authentication protocol descriptors (including HashIDList and DHgIDList).
2. **DH-HMAC-CHAP_Challenge**: Controller replies with T_ID, selected HashID, DHgID, sequence number S1, random challenge C1, and DH exponential (gx mod p). If DHgID is 00h, DH is not used.
3. **DH-HMAC-CHAP_Reply**: Host replies with T_ID, response R1 to C1, and its DH exponential (gy mod p). If bidirectional authentication is requested, it also includes S2, C2 (≠ C1), and DH Value Length is cleared to 0h if DHgID is 00h.
4. **DH-HMAC-CHAP_Success1**: Controller replies with T_ID. If bidirectional auth was requested, it includes R2. Otherwise, it sends AUTH_Failure1 and disconnects on failure.
5. **DH-HMAC-CHAP_Success2** (if bidirectional): Host sends T_ID if host authentication succeeded; otherwise, sends AUTH_Failure2 and disconnects.

If an entity receives an unexpected message, it sends an AUTH_Failure message with reason code 'Authentication failure' and explanation 'Incorrect protocol message', then disconnects. Message payload format must be validated before security computation.

---

### Table 1: Table_8_3_5_5_1_Protocol_Operations

| Symbols | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| NQN<sub>c</sub>, NQN<sub>h</sub> | NQN of the NVM subsystem controller and host |
| K<sub>c</sub>, K<sub>h</sub> | DH-HMAC-CHAP keys of controller and host |
| p, g | Modulus and generator of the chosen DH group |
| x, y | Random DH exponents |
| C<sub>1</sub>, C<sub>2</sub> | Random challenge values |
| C<sub>a1</sub>, C<sub>a2</sub> | Augmented challenge values |
| S<sub>1</sub>, S<sub>2</sub> | 32-bit sequence numbers |
| R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> | Reply values |
| T, ID | Authentication transaction identifier |
| SC, C | Secure channel concatenation indication |
| H( ) | One-way hash function |
| HMAC(K, Str) | HMAC function with key K and string Str |
| || Concatenation operation |
| K<sub>S</sub> | Session key |

---

## 8.3.5.5.2 DH-HMAC-CHAP_Authentication_Protocol_Descriptor

The authentication protocol descriptor for DH-HMAC-CHAP (section 8.3.5.4.1) is defined in Figure 797. It includes supported hash functions and DH groups.

### Hash Functions (Table 2)
- SHA-256 (01h, 32 bytes, 64 bytes block size, RFC 6234) is required.
- SHA-384 (02h), SHA-512 (03h), and vendor-specific (E0h–FEh) are supported.
- Use of SHA-256 may be prohibited by external security policies (e.g., CNSA 1.0 requires SHA-384).

### DH Groups (Table 3)
- 00h: NULL DH group (no exchange, reduces to HMAC-CHAP).
- 01h: 2048-bit (RFC 7919).
- 02h: 3072-bit (RFC 7919).
- 03h–05h: 4096-bit, 6144-bit, 8192-bit (RFC 7919).
- 2048-bit and 3072-bit DH groups are required; 2048-bit may be disabled via mechanism.
- Use of 2048-bit may be prohibited by security policies (e.g., CNSA 1.0 requires ≥3072-bit).

### Descriptor Format (Table 1)
| Bytes | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | AuthID: 01h (DH-HMAC-CHAP) |
| 1 | Reserved |
| 2 | HALEN: HashIDList length (1–30) |
| 3 | DHELEN: DHgIDList length (1–30) |
| 3+HALEN:4 | HashIDList: Array of hash function identifiers |
| 33:4+HALEN | Pad: 0h, if present |
| 33+DHELEN:34 | DHgIDList: Array of DH group identifiers |
| 63:34+DHELEN | PAD1: Padding, 0h, if present |

### Validation Rules
- If HashIDList does not satisfy controller policy (e.g., SHA-256 proposed but SHA-384 required), send AUTH_Failure1 with reason 'Hash function not usable' and disconnect.
- If DHgIDList does not satisfy policy (e.g., only 00h proposed but ≥3072-bit required), send AUTH_Failure1 with reason 'DH group not usable' and disconnect.
- If DHgID is 00h and SC_C ≠ 0, send AUTH_Failure1 with reason 'DH group not usable' and disconnect.

---

## 8.3.5.5.3 DH-HMAC-CHAP_Challenge_Message

Sent from controller to host. Format shown in Figure 800.

- **Hash Length (HL)**: Length (in bytes) of selected hash function (e.g., 32 for SHA-256).
- **HashID**: Selected hash function identifier from Host’s proposed list (01h–03h). Controller selects according to policy.
- **DHgID**: Selected DH group identifier from Host’s list (01h–05h, 00h). If 00h, DH is not used. Must not be 00h if SC_C ≠ 0.
- **DH Value Length (DHVLEN)**: Length (in bytes) of DH exponential; multiple of 4. Set to 0h if DHgID is 00h.
- **Sequence Number (SEQNUM)**: 32-bit S1. Random non-zero initial value. Incremented modulo 232, skipping 0h (i.e., FFFFFFFFh → 00000001h).

sections.title: DH-HMAC-CHAP_Authentication_Verification_Entity
sections.summary:
# 8.3.5.6 DH-HMAC-CHAP Authentication Verification Entity

## 8.3.5.6.1 Overview

A DH-HMAC-CHAP Authentication Verification Entity (AVE) performs authentication verification on behalf of an NVMe entity (host or controller). NVMe entities use the AVE to delegate response verification, exchanging parameters via `DH-HMAC-CHAP_Access-Request` messages. The AVE replies with a `DH-HMAC-CHAP_Access-Result` message (Section 8.3.5.6.3). Use of the AVE is optional and determined by configuration. If used, NVMe entities only require provisioning of their DH-HMAC-CHAP secret and AVE access parameters; no DH-HMAC-CHAP keys are needed for verification. An AVE maintains:
- NVMe entity NQN (NQNe)
- DH-HMAC-CHAP key (Ke)
- PSK shared with AVE (PSKea)

The AVE supports all DH-HMAC-CHAP hash functions. It is identified by an NQN (NQNAVE) for discovery and secure connection establishment.

## 8.3.5.6.2 AVE Connections

NVMe entity–AVE connections use TLS 1.3 with pre-shared key (PSK) authentication (per NVMe over TCP). The PSK (PSKea) is derived from the DH-HMAC-CHAP secret or provisioned:
- **From DH-HMAC-CHAP secret**:  
  1. PRK = HKDF-Extract(0, DH-HMAC-CHAP secret)  
  2. PSKea = HKDF-Expand-Label(PRK, “A-V-Entity” || NQNAVE, NQNe, Length(secret))  
  Uses hash function from secret; requires NQNAVE. Not possible if secret doesn’t specify hash.
- **From configured PSK**:  
  1. PRK = HKDF-Extract(0, configured PSK)  
  2. PSKea = HKDF-Expand-Label(PRK, “A-V-Entity” || NQNAVE, NQNe, Length(PSK))  
  Uses hash from PSK interchange format; defaults to PSK if not specified. Requires NQNAVE.

The TLS connection uses PSKea as Retained PSK, NQNe as host NQN, and NQNAVE as controller NQN. Mandatory/recommended cipher suites are defined in NVMe over TCP. The connection may be reused for multiple verifications and supports TLS heartbeat extension to avoid termination. An AVE may terminate idle connections (e.g., after 10 minutes).

## 8.3.5.6.3 AVE Access Protocol

Communication uses two PDUs over TLS:
- **DH-HMAC-CHAP_Access-Request** (PDU-Type: AEh): Contains transaction parameters.
  - Format (Table 1):
    - Bytes 0–15: Header (Type, Flags, HLEN=08h, PDO, PLEN, ID)
    - 16: Hash Length (HL)
    - 17: HashID
    - 19:18: T_ID (16-bit)
    - 20: SC_C
    - 21: RESPR (‘H’=host, ‘C’=controller)
    - 22: NQNRlen
    - 23: Reserved
    - 27:24: SEQN (Sequence Number S)
    - 27+HL:28: ACV (Augmented Challenge, Ca)
    - 27+2*HL:28+HL: RESPV (Response R)
    - NQNRlen+27+2*HL:28+2*HL: NQNR (Responder NQN)
- **DH-HMAC-CHAP_Access-Result** (PDU-Type: AFh): Returns verification result.
  - Format (Table 2):
    - Bytes 0–15: Header (Type, Flags, HLEN=08h, PDO, PLEN=14h, ID)
    - 16: AuthRes (01h=Success, 02h=Failed)
    - 17: RCODE (00h=None, 01h=Auth failure, 02h=Hash unusable, others=Reserved)
    - 19:18: Reserved

**Authentication Verification Steps** (after receiving Access-Request):
1. Lookup responder’s DH-HMAC-CHAP key (Kr) from NQNR.
2. Compute expected response R’:
   - If Responder’s Role = ‘H’ (host):  
     R’ = HMAC(Kr, Ca || S || T_ID || SC_C || “HostHost” || NQNr || 00h || NQNa)
   - If Responder’s Role = ‘C’ (controller):  
     R’ = HMAC(Kr, Ca || S || T_ID || SC_C || “Controller” || NQNr || 00h || NQNa)
   (NQNa = authenticator NQN, retrieved from TLS identity)
3. Compare R’ with received R:  
   - R’ = R → authentication successful  
   - R’ ≠ R → authentication failed

## 8.3.5.6.4 AVE Discovery

AVE transport addresses can be configured or discovered via a Discovery Controller (e.g., CDC). NVMe entities select randomly from discovered addresses. AVE Discovery is facilitated by the AVE Discovery log page (Section 5.2.12.3.5).

sections.title: Error_Reporting_and_Recovery
sections.summary:
# 9 Error Reporting and Recovery

## Overview  
This section defines the error reporting and recovery mechanisms for the system, ensuring consistent and reliable handling of faults. It specifies error types, reporting formats, recovery procedures, and architectural requirements for error management.

## 9.1 Error Types and Codes  
Errors are categorized into three types:  
- **Fatal Errors**: Cause immediate system termination.  
- **Non-Fatal Errors**: Allow system recovery without shutdown.  
- **Warnings**: Indicate non-critical issues.  

Error codes are 32-bit values structured as:  
- **Type (8 bits)**: 0 = Fatal, 1 = Non-Fatal, 2 = Warning.  
- **Subsystem (8 bits)**: Identifies affected component.  
- **Code (16 bits)**: Specific error identifier.  

Valid error codes: 0x00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF.  
Example: `0x01050001` → Non-Fatal error in Subsystem 5, Code 1.

## 9.2 Error Reporting Mechanism  
- Errors are logged in a dedicated **Error Buffer** of size 512 bytes.  
- Buffer structure:  
  ```  
  [Timestamp (4B)] [Error Code (4B)] [Subsys ID (1B)] [Level (1B)] [Info (408B)]  
  ```  
- Timestamp uses system ticks (1 ms resolution).  
- Critical errors trigger immediate interrupt (IRQ 32).  

## 9.3 Recovery Procedures  
- **Immediate Recovery**: Triggered by non-fatal errors; restarts affected subsystem only.  
- **Graceful Shutdown**: Initiated by fatal errors; saves state to non-volatile memory.  
- **Restart Policy**: Max 3 recovery attempts per error before system halt.  

## 9.4 Error Logging and Diagnostics  
- Error logs are stored in persistent memory (minimum 2048 entries).  
- Each log entry includes:  
  - Timestamp  
  - Error code  
  - Error description (text, up to 128 characters)  
- Diagnostic tools access logs via API: `GetErrorLog(index)` → returns log entry.  

## 9.5 Architecture Requirements  
- **Error Handler Module**: Must respond within 10 ms after error detection.  
- **Redundancy**: Dual independent error detection circuits required.  
- **Fault Tolerance**: System must tolerate single subsystem failure without global crash.  

## 9.6 Recovery Time Requirements  
| Error Type        | Max Recovery Time |  
|-------------------|-------------------|  
| Non-Fatal         | 200 ms            |  
| Fatal (Graceful)  | 1000 ms           |  
| Warning           | None (ignored)    |  

## 9.7 Error Code Table  
| Code (Hex) | Description                  | Type    |  
|------------|------------------------------|---------|  
| 0x01000001 | Memory access violation      | Non-Fatal |  
| 0x01000002 | Invalid command received     | Non-Fatal |  
| 0x02010001 | Power supply fluctuation     | Warning  |  
| 0x00050001 | Critical stack overflow      | Fatal   |  

> **Note**: All error codes must be documented in the system's public error reference.

sections.title: Command_and_Queue_Error_Handling
sections.summary:
# 9.1 Command and Queue Error Handling

In the case of serious error conditions—such as a command specifying an invalid Completion Queue—the associated Submission Queue or Completion Queue may be compromised. The host should delete the affected queue(s). Deleting a Submission Queue aborts all outstanding commands associated with it. Deleting either queue type releases associated resources. After deletion, the host must recreate the queue(s) to resume operation.

For serious error conditions involving Admin commands, or if a completion is not received for a queue deletion, the entire controller must be reset using a Controller Level Reset.

For most command errors, the queues themselves are not affected. The host and controller continue processing commands. The host may choose to retry the failed command at its discretion; the Retry bit in the completion queue entry indicates whether a retry may succeed.

sections.title: Media_and_Data_Error_Handling
sections.summary:
# 9.2 Media and Data Error Handling

- **Section ID**: 9.2 | **Page**: 766-766  
- When a command cannot be performed on NVM media, it completes with a media error and the appropriate status code.
- **Read Errors** (e.g., End-to-end Guard Check Error, Unrecovered Read Error):  
  - Controller may stop or continue DMA transfer into memory.  
  - Host must ignore data in memory for commands completing with such errors.
- **Write Errors** (e.g., internal error, End-to-end Guard Check Error, End-to-end Application Tag Check Error):  
  - Controller may stop or complete the DMA transfer.
- Additional I/O Command Set-specific error handling is defined in applicable NVM Express I/O Command Set specifications.

sections.title: Memory_Error_Handling
sections.summary:
# 9.3 Memory Error Handling

For PCI Express implementations, memory errors—such as target abort, master abort, and parity—may cause the controller to stop processing the currently executing command. These are serious errors requiring host intervention for recovery.

A **master abort** or **target abort** occurs when the host provides the controller with an invalid memory address. In such cases, the controller aborts the command with a **Data Transfer Error** status code.

sections.title: Internal_Controller_Error_Handling
sections.summary:
## 9.4 Internal Controller Error Handling

- **Section ID**: 9.4 | **Page**: 766-766  
- If a controller-level failure (e.g., DRAM failure) occurs during command processing, the controller must abort the command with a **status code of Internal Error**.  
- Any data transfer associated with the command may be **incomplete or incorrect**; such data must not be used except for error reporting or diagnosis.  
- The host may **re-submit the command** or **indicate an error** to higher-level software.

sections.title: Controller_Fatal_Status_Condition
sections.summary:
### 9.5 Controller Fatal Status Condition

- **CSTS.CFS Bit**: Set to `1` when a serious error prevents communication via completion queues (Admin or I/O). Indicates the host should reset and re-initialize the controller.
- **No Interrupt**: The condition does not trigger an interrupt. Hosts should check CSTS.CFS if timeouts or repeated errors occur.
- **Controller Reset**: If CSTS.CFS is set on any controller in the NVM subsystem, the host must issue a **Controller Level Reset**.
- **NVM Subsystem Reset (NSSR)**: If the Controller Reset does not clear the condition, and NSSR is supported, the host may initiate NSSR.
- **NSSR Impact**: May cause PCI Express links to go down, potentially causing system instability (e.g., OS/hypervisor crashes).
- **Restriction**: Hosts using **Firmware First Error Handling** (per ACPI Specification) must **not** use NSSR for recovery from CFS conditions.

sections.title: Communication_Loss_Handling
sections.summary:
# 9.6 Communication_Loss_Handling

**Section ID**: 9.6 | **Page**: 767-767

If the host loses communication with a controller, it cannot receive completions (CQEs) for outstanding commands (see Section 3.4.5). If the host can use another controller or re-establish communication with the original controller, it is strongly recommended to follow the procedures in this section to prevent user data corruption or unintended NVM subsystem state changes.

Host recovery from communication loss involves three components:
- **Detection of communication loss**: Described in Section 9.6.1.
- **Determination that no further controller processing of outstanding commands is possible**: Described in Section 9.6.2.
- **Retry of outstanding commands (if any)**: Described in Section 9.6.3.

These components are interdependent: detection of communication loss must occur before determining that no further processing is possible. Retries of commands that modify user data or subsystem state can corrupt data or cause unintended changes unless the host confirms that the controller is no longer processing the commands (as specified in Section 9.6.2).

sections.title: Host_Communication_Loss_with_a_Controller
sections.summary:
# 9.6.1 Host Communication Loss with a Controller

A host determines that communication has been lost with a controller if:

- The host detects a Keep Alive Timeout (refer to section 3.9);
- For message-based transports, the host or the controller terminates the NVMe Transport connection on which the command was sent (refer to section 3.3.2.4);
- The host detects a transport connection loss using methods outside the scope of this specification (e.g., the transport notifies the host of a loss of communication either with the controller to which the command was submitted or with the queue on which the command was sent); or
- The host reads the Lost Host Communication log page (refer to section 5.2.12.3.2) via another controller in the same NVM subsystem and finds an entry containing the controller ID of that first controller and the value of the Controller Instance Uniquifier (CIU) field is the same as the value of the CIU field in the Identify Controller data structure for that controller.

Any action that terminates the NVMe Transport connection (e.g., a host reboot) causes the host to lose communication with a controller.  

A controller may detect a loss of communication at a different time (e.g., later) than the host detects that loss of communication. As explained in section 9.6.2.1, additional time may be required for the controller to stop processing commands after the controller detects a loss of communication.

sections.title: End_of_Controller_Processing_of_Outstanding_Comman
sections.summary:
## 9.6.2 End of Controller Processing of Outstanding Commands

### Overview
This section defines how a host determines that no further controller processing of outstanding commands is possible after a communication loss. When communication is lost, outstanding commands are those for which the host cannot receive a Completion Queue Entry (CQE), as defined in Section 3.4.5. Some commands (e.g., Sanitize) initiate background operations that can continue after the host loses communication. In such cases, additional steps (e.g., commands to a different controller) are needed to track completion.

### Key Recovery Mechanisms
To determine that no further processing of outstanding commands is possible, the host must use one or more recovery mechanisms:

- **Cross-Controller Reset Recovery (Section 9.6.2.2)**:  
  Available if the host has an association with a different message-based controller and both support this feature. This method is expected to complete faster than Time-Based Recovery. The host should use it if available.

- **Time-Based Recovery (Section 9.6.2.1)**:  
  Always available. The host must perform this in parallel with Cross-Controller Reset Recovery (if used) to avoid delays if Cross-Controller Reset fails.

The host should use these recovery methods in sequence or in parallel to ensure confirmation that no further processing is occurring.

sections.title: Time-Based_Recovery
sections.summary:
# 9.6.2.1 Time-Based Recovery

For **Time-Based Recovery**, the host performs the following steps:

1. **Terminate association and transport connections** (skipped for memory-based transports).
2. **Detect loss of communication** using at least one of the following methods:
   - a. **Command-Based Keep Alive**: Wait ≥ 2 × KATT from the time of the most recent Keep Alive Command (Section 3.9.3.1).
   - b. **Traffic-Based Keep Alive**: Wait ≥ 3 × KATT from the time of the most recent command (Section 3.9.4.1).
   - c. **Cross-Controller Reset Log Page** (Section 5.2.12.3.1):
     - Read on another controller in the same NVM subsystem.
     - Detection indicated if the log entry contains:
       - i. Controller ID of this controller.
       - ii. CIU matching the Identify Controller CIU.
       - iii. Cross-Controller Reset Status = Failed.
       - iv. Controller Level Reset Initiated bit = 1.
   - d. **Lost Host Communication Log Page** (Section 5.2.12.3.2):
     - Read on another controller in the same NVM subsystem.
     - Detection indicated if log entry contains:
       - i. Controller ID of this controller.
       - ii. CIU matching the Identify Controller CIU.
   - e. Receive transport-specific notification (e.g., fabric notification, PCIe surprise link down).
3. **Wait for controller to stop processing commands** using one of:
   - a. If CQT (Figure 328) is non-zero: Wait for the CQT value (in milliseconds).
   - b. If CQT = 0h: Wait for implementation-specific time (e.g., 10 seconds); configurable administratively.

> **Note**: The 2 × KATT and 3 × KATT waiting times assume transport delays ≤ KATT. The controller detects Keep Alive Timeout in ≤ 1 × KATT for Command-Based and ≤ 2 × KATT for Traffic-Based, resulting in a total delay of ≤ 2 × KATT and ≤ 3 × KATT, respectively.

sections.title: Cross-Controller_Reset_Recovery,_Message-Based_Tra
sections.summary:
# 9.6.2.2 Cross-Controller Reset Recovery, Message-Based Transports

This section describes **Cross-Controller Reset Recovery** for **message-based transport models**, enabling a host to recover from communication loss with an **Impacted Controller** using a **Source Controller** within the same NVM subsystem, as defined in section 5.4.3.

### Key Steps:
1. **Terminate** the association and transport connections with the Impacted Controller.
2. Submit a **Cross-Controller Reset command** to the Source Controller, specifying the Impacted Controller and including:
   - **CIU field** (Controller Instance Unit)
   - **CIRNL field** (Controller Instance Reset Number Logical)
   - **CIRNU field** (Controller Instance Reset Number Unit)
3. **Determine completion** of the operation by:
   - Receiving a **CQE** with the **Immediate Reset Successful (IRS)** bit set to `1`, or
   - Reading the **Cross-Controller Reset log page** (section 5.2.12.3.1), where the **Cross-Controller Reset Status (CCRS)** field is **not** "In Progress" (indicates success or failure).

The host may poll the log page or respond to a **Cross-Controller Reset Completed asynchronous event**.

### Recovery:
- If successful, the host may **recover outstanding commands** to the Impacted Controller **without waiting** for the association termination to complete.
- If the **CCRS field is "Failed"**, the host may retry Cross-Controller Reset Recovery per section 8.3.3.
- If all attempts fail, use **Time-Based Recovery** (section 9.6.2.1).

sections.title: Command_Retry_After_Communication_Loss
sections.summary:
## 9.6.3 Command Retry After Communication Loss

If the host loses communication with a controller, it cannot receive completion (CQE) for outstanding commands. If communication is reestablished or another controller is used, the host may retry outstanding commands to recover. Hosts are strongly recommended to follow the procedures in this section to avoid data corruption or unintended NVM subsystem state changes (e.g., Reservation state, per section 8.1.24).

For retry purposes, outstanding commands fall into one of three categories based on idempotency and whether they modify user data or NVM subsystem state:
- **Unrestricted Retry**
- **Delayed Retry**
- **State-Dependent Retry**

Section 9.6.3.2 defines these categories and describes requirements and restrictions for retrying commands in each category.

sections.title: Idempotent_Commands
sections.summary:
### 9.6.3.1 Idempotent Commands

**Definition**: An idempotent command produces the same end state on the NVM subsystem and returns the same results if resubmitted one or more times with no intervening commands. Ancillary state changes (e.g., statistics tracking) do not affect idempotency.

**Results Include**:
- Status code (excluding transient or error conditions, e.g., due to communication loss)
- Data returned to the host
- NVM subsystem changes to user data or state (e.g., reservation state, feature contents)

**Examples**:
- **Idempotent**: Read command to a valid LBA in a namespace returns the same data with success on repeated submission.
- **Idempotent**: Write command to a valid LBA in a namespace writes the same data on repeated submission.

**Non-Idempotent Examples**:
- **Namespace Management command** (Section 5.2.21): Creating a namespace is not idempotent; repeated submissions create additional namespaces with different identifiers.
- **Reservation Register command** (Section 7.6): Unregistering a host is not idempotent; repeated submission attempts to unregister a host already unregistered, returning an error.

sections.title: Command_Retry_Categories_and_Requirements
sections.summary:
# 9.6.3.2 Command Retry Categories and Requirements

For command retry, outstanding commands are categorized into three types:

- **Unrestricted Retry**: Idempotent commands that do not affect user data or NVM subsystem state (e.g., NVM Command Set Read). These commands may be retried immediately after communication loss. The following bits in the **Commands Supported and Effects** log page (Figure 214) must be cleared to '0':
  - Controller Capability Change (CCC)
  - Namespace Inventory Change (NIC)
  - Namespace Capability Change (NCC)
  - Logical Block Content Change (LBCC)
  If any of these bits is '1', the command is not Unrestricted Retry.

- **Delayed Retry**: Idempotent commands that change user data or NVM subsystem state (e.g., NVM Command Set Write), but do not affect other hosts' behavior. The host must **not report completion or error status** to higher-level software until no further controller processing of the command (including retries) is possible. Retries must be delayed until the original command and prior retries cannot be further processed. Violating this may cause **user data corruption**.

- **State-Dependent Retry**: Non-idempotent commands (e.g., Namespace Management) or idempotent commands that affect other hosts' behavior. Hosts must **not retry** without determining the recovery action, which requires higher-level software due to potential differences in behavior, duplication, or impact on other hosts. The host must **not report completion or error status** until no further processing is possible. Violating this may cause **user data corruption or unintended NVM subsystem state changes**.

In all cases, hosts may treat any command as a more restrictive category (e.g., treat Unrestricted Retry as Delayed or State-Dependent). The key requirement is to **avoid reporting results before ensuring no further controller processing** to prevent data corruption or unintended state changes.

sections.title: Annex_A._Sanitize_Operation_Considerations_(Inform
sections.summary:
# Annex A. Sanitize Operation Considerations (Informative)

## Overview

This section outlines considerations for sanitize operations, defining key terms and detailing architectural requirements for secure data sanitization processes.

## Key Definitions

- **Sanitize Operation**: A process to securely erase or render data irrecoverable, ensuring no residual data remains accessible after the operation.

## Architectural Requirements

- **Sanitize Scope**:
  - Applies to all user-accessible storage media (e.g., internal flash, persistent memory).
  - Includes data in both active and inactive states (e.g., cached, encrypted, or dormant).

- **Sanitize Methods**:
  - **Logical Sanitize**: Uses software-based methods (e.g., overwrite with zero or random patterns).
  - **Physical Sanitize**: Involves hardware-based destruction (e.g., power cycling, secure erase commands).

- **Sanitize Triggers**:
  - Initiated via API call or device command.
  - Must be supported during power-on and post-reset states.

## Performance Requirements

- **Sanitize Duration**:
  - For logical sanitize: Maximum 10 seconds per gigabyte of storage.
  - For physical sanitize: Maximum 5 seconds per gigabyte.

## Data Integrity

- **Validation**:
  - Post-sanitize verification required to ensure data is fully erased.
  - Verification must pass with 100% success rate.

## Security

- **Sanitize Access Control**:
  - Only authenticated and authorized entities may initiate sanitize.
  - Access requires cryptographic key or role-based permissions.

## Implementation Notes

- **Sanitize Operation Table**:

| Component         | Supported Sanitize Method | Max Time per GB |
|-------------------|----------------------------|------------------|
| Internal Flash    | Logical & Physical         | 10 s / GB        |
| Persistent Memory | Logical & Physical         | 5 s / GB         |
| External Storage  | Logical Only               | 10 s / GB        |

sections.title: A.1_Overview
sections.summary:
**Section A.1 Overview**

- The **Sanitize command** initiates a sanitize operation that makes all user data written to the sanitization target inaccessible, per **IEEE Std 2883** definition of purging.
- Proving successful purging of all user data is **very difficult**.
- This annex provides **context and considerations** for understanding sanitize operation results and **practical limitations** for auditing the operation’s outcome.

sections.title: A.2_Hidden_Storage_(Overprovisioning)
sections.summary:
### A.2 Hidden Storage (Overprovisioning)

- **Definition**: Hidden storage refers to physical storage in NVMe SSDs that is not addressable through the interface, typically used for overprovisioning.
- **Purpose**: Used by vendors for enhancing endurance, improving performance, and enabling retirement of bad or worn-out storage without impacting accessible capacity.
- **Accessibility**: This excess and retired storage is not accessible via the interface and thus not directly auditable.
- **Sanitization Challenge**: Sanitization operations purge only the **accessible** physical storage; hidden storage (including overprovisioned and retired areas) is not guaranteed to be purged.
- **Key Requirement**: Since hidden storage is not observable, it is difficult to ensure complete sanitization across the entire physical storage of the device.
- **Implication**: Only accessible storage can be verified for successful sanitization.

sections.title: A.3_Integrity_checks_and_No-Deallocate_After_Sanit
sections.summary:
# NoID A.3_Integrity_checks_and_No-Deallocate_After_Sanit

### A.3 Integrity checks and No-Deallocate After Sanitize

The Sanitize command may trigger internal integrity checks or scramble vendor-specific data formats, leading to error responses instead of readable data. To enable readable media after sanitization, controllers may perform additional write operations to media allocated for user data (see Section 8.1.26.2), but this increases media wear and obscures forensic auditability. Process and forensic audits are only effective if the **No-Deallocate After Sanitize bit** is set to '1' in both cases.

The Sanitize command (introduced in NVMe Rev 1.3) allows preventing deallocation of sanitized media for observation. However, some architectures (e.g., integrity checking circuitry) can interfere with observing sanitize results. NVMe Rev 1.4 adds features to address this: extended sanitization capability information, a new asynchronous event, and configuration of responses to No-Deallocate After Sanitize requests, supporting both new and legacy systems.

These integrity check issues do not occur if the sanitization target is in the **Media Verification state** (Section 8.1.26.4.6). In this state, Read commands do not return errors due to integrity check failures (as specified in the Media Verification section of the NVMe NVM Command Set Specification), provided the **Enter Media Verification State (EMVS)** bit was set to '1' when entering the state.

sections.title: A.4_Bad_Media_and_Vendor_Specific_NAND_Use
sections.summary:
# NoID A.4_Bad_Media_and_Vendor_Specific_NAND_Use

## Overview
NVM Express does not support auditing whether media with unsanitized data (e.g., bad physical blocks) has been removed from the usable addressable storage pool.

## Key Issues
- **Physical removal** of storage components post-sanitize is sometimes used in labs to verify sanitization.
- This method **loses critical context**, including:
  - a) Encoding for zero’s/one’s balance
  - b) Identification of components containing firmware or non-data information
  - c) Determination of which media has been retired and cannot be sanitized

## Implication
This approach is **not reliable** for audit purposes due to loss of device-specific and media-level context.

sections.title: Annex_B._Host_Considerations_(Informative)
sections.summary:
# NoID Annex_B._Host_Considerations_(Informative)

## Annex B. Host Considerations (Informative)

This section provides informal guidance on host considerations for system design, focusing on architectural and operational aspects. It does not define requirements but offers insights to support implementation.

- **Key Requirement**: Hosts must ensure proper handling of identifier-free (NoID) communication, particularly in environments where unique identifiers are not used or are dynamically assigned.
- **Architectural Details**: 
  - Hosts should support dynamic resolution of endpoint references, especially in scalable or decentralized systems.
  - Consideration is given to security implications, such as mitigating spoofing or replay attacks without identifiers.
- **Operational Considerations**:
  - Hosts may need to maintain transient state for tracking communications in the absence of persistent identifiers.
  - Performance impact of identifier-free operations must be evaluated, particularly in high-throughput or low-latency scenarios.
- **Table Reference**:
  - Table B.1: Example of Host State Management in NoID Environment  
    | Component       | State Tracking | Frequency | Impact |
    |-----------------|----------------|-----------|--------|
    | Message Queue   | High           | Real-time | High   |
    | Session Cache   | Medium         | Periodic  | Medium |
    | Security Log    | Low            | Event-based | Low   |

sections.title: B.1_Basic_Steps_when_Building_a_Command
sections.summary:
# B.1 Basic Steps when Building a Command

When the host builds a command for the controller to execute, it first ensures the Submission Queue (SQ) is not full. The SQ is full when the number of entries is one less than the queue size. Once an empty slot (pFreeSlot) is available:

1. The host builds a command at `SQ[pFreeSlot]` with:
   a. **CDW0.OPC**: Set to the appropriate command to be executed by the controller.
   b. **CDW0.FUSE**: Set to the appropriate value, depending on whether the command is a fused operation.
   c. **CDW0.CID**: Set to a unique identifier for the command when combined with the Submission Queue identifier.
   d. **NSID**: Set to the namespace the command applies to.
   e. **MPTR**: Filled with the offset to the beginning of the Metadata Region, if there is a data transfer and the namespace format contains metadata as a separate buffer.
   f. **PRP1 and/or PRP2** (or **SGL Entry 1** if SGLs are used): Set to the source/destination of data transfer, if there is a data transfer.
   g. **CDW10 – CDW15**: Set to any command-specific information.

2. The host then performs a transport-specific action to submit the command for processing.

sections.title: B.2_Creating_an_I_O_Submission_Queue
sections.summary:
# NoID B.2 Creating an I/O Submission Queue

This section describes how the host creates an I/O Submission Queue (SQ) using non-contiguous PRP entries, valid only if the controller supports non-contiguous queues via `CAP.CQR`.

### Key Steps:
- Prior to creating an SQ, the host must create the corresponding I/O Completion Queue (CQ) using the *Create I/O Completion Queue* command.
- The **Create I/O Submission Queue** command is built in the next free Admin Submission Queue command location.

### Command Attributes:
- **CDW0.OPC** = `01h`
- **CDW0.FUSE** = `00b` (not a fused operation)
- **CDW0.CID** = free command identifier
- **NSID** = `0h` (SQs are not namespace-specific)
- **MPTR** = `0h` (no metadata used)
- **PRP1** = physical address of the PRP List (see Figure 815 for structure)
- **PRP2** = `0h` (PRP Entry 2 not used)
- **CDW10.QSIZE** = queue size in entries (e.g., `191` = 192 entries); must not exceed `CAP.MQES`
- **CDW10.QID** = Submission Queue identifier
- **CDW11.CQID** = I/O Completion Queue identifier for command completions
- **CDW11.QPRIO** = `10b` (Medium priority)
- **CDW11.PC** = `0` (data buffer is not physically contiguous)

### Additional Requirements:
- Host must perform a transport-specific action to submit the command.
- The PRP List must remain unmodified in host memory until the SQ is deleted.

### Figure:
- **Figure 815**: PRP List structure for an I/O Submission Queue (three entries).

sections.title: B.3_Executing_a_Fused_Operation
sections.summary:
# B.3 Executing a Fused Operation

This section describes the execution of a fused operation (Compare and Write) for 16 KiB of data, using two commands in adjacent I/O Submission Queue entries.

### Key Requirements
- **Total Data Size**: 16 KiB  
- **Logical Block Size**: 4 KiB  
- **End-to-End Protection**: Not enabled  
- **Commands**:  
  - `CMD0` (Compare, OPC = 05h)  
  - `CMD1` (Write, OPC = 01h)  
- **Fusion Indicators**:  
  - `CMD0.CDW0.FUSE = 01b` (First command)  
  - `CMD1.CDW0.FUSE = 10b` (Second command)  
- **Shared Parameters**:  
  - `CMD1.NSID = CMD0.NSID`  
  - `CMD1.CDW10.SLBA = CMD0.CDW10.SLBA`  
  - `CMD1.CDW12.NLB = CMD0.CDW12.NLB = 3h` (4 blocks, 4 KiB each)  
- **Data Addressing**:  
  - **PRP**: `CMD0.PRP1` and `CMD0.PRP2` (PRP List, 3 entries), same for `CMD1`  
  - **SGL**: `CMD0.SGL1` and `CMD1.SGL1` (segment descriptors)  
- **Flags**:  
  - `LR = 0` (apply error recovery)  
  - `FUA = 0` (data may be read/written from cache)  
  - `PRINFO = 0h`, `CDW14 = 0h`, `CDW15 = 0h` (no E2E protection)  
- **Submission**: Both commands submitted in a single transport-specific action.  

**Figure 816** illustrates a PRP List with three entries for the Compare command.

sections.title: B.4_Asynchronous_Event_Request_Host_Recommendation
sections.summary:
# NoID B.4_Asynchronous_Event_Request_Host_Recommendation

## B.4 Asynchronous Event Request Host Recommendations

The host performs the following steps upon completion of an Asynchronous Event Request command (Section 3.5.1, step 12):

1. **Check Log Page Disable Capability**:  
   If the reported Log Page supports disabling events via the *Asynchronous Event Configuration* feature (Section 5.2.26.1.5), the host issues a **Set Features** command to disable reporting of all events using that Log Page. The host must wait for the command to complete.

2. **Retrieve Log Page**:  
   The host issues a **Get Log Page** command to retrieve the Log Page reported in the event. The host must wait for completion.

3. **Parse Log Page and Re-enable Events**:  
   - If the condition is **not persistent**, re-enable all asynchronous events using that Log Page via a **Set Features** command.  
   - If the condition is **persistent**, re-enable all asynchronous events except the one(s) reported in the Log Page, using a **Set Features** command.

4. **Resume Asynchronous Event Requests**:  
   Issue an **Asynchronous Event Request** command to restore the number of outstanding commands to `n`.

5. **Re-enable Specific Events (if disabled)**:  
   If event reporting was disabled, enable reporting of the event(s) using the **Asynchronous Event Configuration** feature. If the condition may persist (e.g., spare below threshold), continue monitoring to determine if re-enabling is appropriate.

sections.title: B.5_Updating_Controller_Doorbell_Properties_using
sections.summary:
### B.5 Updating Controller Doorbell Properties using a Shadow Doorbell Buffer

This section defines the mechanism for updating doorbell properties in a controller using a shadow doorbell buffer. The shadow buffer is used to maintain consistent and atomic updates to doorbell properties, ensuring reliability during concurrent operations.

**Key Requirements:**
- Doorbell properties (e.g., base address, size, vector, interrupt state) must be updated atomically to prevent race conditions.
- The shadow doorbell buffer must mirror the actual doorbell hardware state.
- Updates to the shadow buffer must precede corresponding hardware writes.

**Architecture:**
- The shadow buffer is stored in controller memory and accessed via a pointer maintained by the driver.
- The size of the shadow buffer is determined by the number of doorbells supported, with each doorbell entry containing:
  - **Base Address (64-bit):** Physical address of the doorbell.
  - **Size (32-bit):** Size of the doorbell region in bytes.
  - **Vector (32-bit):** Interrupt vector associated with the doorbell.
  - **Interrupt State (32-bit):** Current interrupt enable status (0 = disabled, 1 = enabled).
- Updates to the shadow buffer must be followed by a hardware synchronization step, typically through a write to a designated synchronization register.

**Update Procedure:**
1. Lock the shadow buffer update mechanism.
2. Modify the shadow buffer entry for the target doorbell with the new properties.
3. Write a synchronization value to a controller register to trigger hardware update.
4. Unlock the update mechanism.

**Notes:**
- The synchronization register is located at offset `0x100` in the controller's memory-mapped I/O space.
- A full update cycle must complete within 10 microseconds to ensure real-time responsiveness.

sections.title: B.5.1._Shadow_Doorbell_Buffer_Overview
sections.summary:
### B.5.1. Shadow Doorbell Buffer Overview

- **Purpose**: Enhances host performance in virtualized environments for emulated controllers supporting the Doorbell Buffer Config command (Section 5.3.5).
- **Mechanism**: Host submits commands by updating entries in the Shadow Doorbell buffer instead of the controller’s doorbell property.
- **Trigger for Doorbell Update**: If updating a Shadow Doorbell buffer entry changes its value from ≤ to > the corresponding EventIdx buffer value, the host must also update the controller's doorbell property to match the new Shadow Doorbell value.
- **Queue Wrap**: Queue wrap conditions must be considered in all comparisons.
- **Controller Behavior**: The controller may read the Shadow Doorbell buffer and update the EventIdx buffer at any time (e.g., before the host updates the controller's doorbell property).

sections.title: B.5.2._Example_Algorithm_for_Controller_Doorbell_P
sections.summary:
### B.5.2. Example Algorithm for Controller Doorbell Property Updates

The host determines whether to update the controller doorbell property using modular arithmetic with the queue depth as the modulus. Key steps:

- Compute **X** = (new doorbell value − EventIdx) mod queue depth  
- Compute **Y** = (new doorbell value − old doorbell value in shadow buffer) mod queue depth  

If **X ≤ Y**, the controller doorbell property is updated with the new doorbell value.

sections.title: B.6_Examples_of_Incorrect_Command_Retry_Handling_A
sections.summary:
## B.6 Examples of Incorrect Command Retry Handling After Communication Loss

### Overview
Section 9.6.3 requires hosts to handle command retries after communication loss with caution, as the controller’s processing status for an outstanding command is unknown. Retrying commands without considering their side effects can lead to unintended behavior. This section illustrates problematic scenarios caused by improper retry handling.

### Key Requirement
- Hosts must not unconditionally retry commands after communication loss if the command may have already been partially or fully processed.
- Commands must be retry-safe; otherwise, re-execution risks data inconsistency or system errors.

### Architectural Details
- Communication loss creates uncertainty about command completion.
- Retrying non-idempotent commands can result in unintended side effects (e.g., repeated writes, transaction commits).

### Examples (Summary)
- **Command Retrying Without Validation**: Retrying a write command after communication loss may result in duplicate data entries.
- **Non-Idempotent Commands**: Commands that change system state (e.g., deletion, transaction commit) must not be retried blindly.
- **Controller State Uncertainty**: The host cannot determine if the controller executed the command, partially executed it, or failed to process it.

> **Reference**: Section 9.6.3 of the specification governs proper command retry behavior after communication loss.

sections.title: B.6.1._Write_after_Write
sections.summary:
# NoID B.6.1._Write_after_Write

## B.6.1. Write after Write

### Overview
In the scenario described in Figure 817, a host loses communication with Controller 1 while executing an idempotent command (e.g., NVM Command Set Write) that changes user data at location X to A. The following sequence occurs:

- The host retries the command on Controller 2, which succeeds quickly.
- After the retry completes, the host submits a new command to change the user data at location X to B.
- Meanwhile, Controller 1 processes the original command, and its change (to A) takes effect after the data has already been changed to B.

**Result**: The final value at location X is A, despite the host later writing B, leading to **data corruption**.

### Key Requirement
For idempotent commands that modify user data or NVM subsystem state, the host **must not report the command completion** (including retries) to higher-level software until it can confirm that no further controller processing of the command or any retry is possible (see Section 9.6.2).

### Figure Reference
- **Figure 817**: Visualizes the "Write after Write" race condition leading to data corruption.

sections.title: B.6.2._Non-Idempotent_Command
sections.summary:
# NoID B.6.2._Non-Idempotent_Command

### B.6.2. Non-Idempotent Command

- **Section ID**: | **Page**: 780-780  
- **Definition**: A non-idempotent command is one that, if repeated, may cause unintended changes to the NVM subsystem state (e.g., creating duplicate namespaces).  
- **Example**: In Figure 818, a host sends a Namespace Management command to create a namespace to Controller 1 but loses communication. The host retries the command on Controller 2, resulting in a second namespace being created.  
- **Key Requirement**: Higher-level software (e.g., application, filesystem, or database) must ensure that retrying a non-idempotent command does not result in unintended state changes (e.g., multiple namespaces).  
- **Architectural Note**: The host must confirm that the original command did not complete on the first controller (refer to Section 9.6.2) before retrying on another controller.  
- **Reference**: Section 5.2.21 for Namespace Management command details.  
- **Figure**: Figure 818 illustrates the scenario.  

*Note: No table data or numerical values are included in this section.*

sections.title: B.6.3._Retried_Command_Does_Not_Succeed
sections.summary:
### B.6.3. Retried Command Does Not Succeed

- **Scenario**: The host loses communication with Controller 1 after sending a Reservation Register command that unregisters the host (see section 7.6).
- **Host Action**: Ensures no further processing of the command by the original controller (see section 9.6.2), then retries the command on Controller 2.
- **Result**: Since the original command already unregistered the host, the host is no longer a registrant. Controller 2 returns a **Reservation Conflict** status code (see section 8.1.24.4).
- **Key Point**: Demonstrates that a non-idempotent command may fail on retry if the original command has already been processed.
- **Analogous Case**: Compare and Write fused operation (non-idempotent) in the NVM Express NVM Command Set Specification.

sections.title: B.6.4._Retried_Command_Affects_Another_Host
sections.summary:
## B.6.4. Retried Command Affects Another Host

### Summary

This section highlights the risks of retrying commands that can affect the behavior of other hosts in a multi-host NVMe environment. It presents a scenario where two hosts use a shared location (Location X) for coordination:

- **Step A**: Host 1 writes value **A** to Location X to indicate completion.
- **Issue**: Host 1 experiences communication loss and does not receive confirmation.
- **Consequence**: Host 2 observes **A**, performs **Step B**, and writes **B** to Location X.
- **Problem**: Host 1 retries writing **A**, overwriting **B** — causing incorrect state.

### Key Requirements and Constraints

- **Command Retry Risk**: Retrying commands that modify shared state (e.g., write to shared location) after communication loss can **overwrite progress made by other hosts**.
- **Higher-Level Coordination**: Using NVMe commands (e.g., NVM Write) for coordination/synchronization among hosts is **strongly discouraged**.
- **Safe Alternatives**:
  - **Reservations** (see Section 8.1.24)
  - **Compare and Write fused operations** (see NVM Command Set Specification)
- **State-Modifying Commands**: Commands that alter NVMe subsystem state (e.g., `Set Features`) with scope visible to other hosts (per Figure 403) may affect behavior of other hosts. These **must not be used for coordination**.

> **Critical Insight**: Retries of commands that modify shared or observable state can lead to **loss of coordination integrity**. Use proper coordination primitives instead.

sections.title: Annex_C._Power_Management_and_Consumption_(Informa
sections.summary:
# Annex C. Power Management and Consumption (Informative)

**Scope**: NVM Express power management covers controller power control and reporting (Section 5.2.26.1.2). Transport power management (e.g., PCIe, RDMA) is defined in applicable NVM Express Transport specifications.

**Key Features**:
- Power Management (Section 5.2.26.1.2, Section 8.1.18)
- Autonomous Power State Transition (Section 5.2.26.1.6, Section 8.1.18.2)
- Non-Operational Power State Configuration (Section 5.2.26.1.10, Section 8.1.18.1)
- Spinup Control (Section 5.2.26.1.18)
- NVM subsystem workloads (Section 8.1.18.3)
- Runtime D3 transitions (Section 8.1.18.4)

**Thermal Management Interactions**:
- Temperature Threshold (Section 5.2.26.1.3)
- Host Controlled Thermal Management (Section 5.2.26.1.9, Section 8.1.18.5)
- Access to host memory buffer (Section 5.2.26.2.4) prohibited in non-operational power state

**Reporting Mechanisms**:
- **Properties**:
  - Controller Power Scope (CAP.CPS) (Figure 36)
- **Identify Controller Data Structure Fields (Figure 328)**:
  - RTD3 Resume Latency (RTD3R)
  - RTD3 Entry Latency (RTD3E)
  - Non-Operational Power State Permissive Mode
  - Number of Power States Support (NPSS)
  - Autonomous Power State Transition Attributes (APSTA)
  - Power State 0 Descriptor (PSD0) to Power State 31 Descriptor (PSD31) (Figure 329)
- **Features**:
  - Power Management
  - Temperature Threshold
  - Autonomous Power State Transition
  - Non-Operational Power State Configuration
  - Host Controlled Thermal Management
  - Host Memory Buffer
  - Spinup Control
- **Log Pages**:
  - SMART / Health Information log page fields:
    - Thermal Management Temperature [1-2] Transition Count
    - Total Time For Thermal Management Temperature [1-2]
  - Persistent Event Log fields (Section 5.2.12.1.14)
